topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on European public health context; digital health competencies may differ from private sector or Australian health systems in governance and regulatory requirements.
takeaways: Identify which digital competencies (technical, data literacy, change management) are most critical for your public health or health-adjacent workforce, then map gaps in your current capability development programs.

Use the framework to benchmark your organisation's digital upskilling approach against European standards, but adapt priorities to reflect Australian regulatory environment and health sector structure.

articles.title: The application of artificial intelligence in the context of person-centred care – a discourse on pitfalls and possibilities - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The application of artificial intelligence in the context of person-centred care – a discourse on pitfalls and possibilities  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — a discourse paper examining AI in person-centred care contexts, likely drawing on published literature rather than primary data. Applicability depends on the specific care sectors and jurisdictions discussed, which are not evident from the title alone.
takeaways: Understand both the opportunities and risks of AI in person-centred care before implementation — this framing helps you anticipate pitfalls and design safer AI adoption strategies in your organisation.
Person-centred care principles should guide AI literacy efforts; ensure teams understand how AI tools either support or undermine individualised, dignified care practices.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focused on middle school education context. Applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development requires careful adaptation, as pedagogical approaches differ significantly between secondary education and professional settings.
takeaways: Consider how foundational AI competencies (beyond technical skills) should be sequenced and integrated into broader digital literacy programmes — a framework approach may be more effective than siloed AI training.

Middle school frameworks suggest starting with conceptual understanding of how AI works before moving to practical application — this staged approach may inform how you structure AI capability development for employees with varying technical backgrounds.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's analysis draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but findings reflect primarily large enterprises and may not apply uniformly to SMEs or non-Western contexts.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability challenge, not just a technology implementation; prioritise upskilling and role redesign alongside tool deployment.
Identify which roles will be augmented (requiring new AI-adjacent skills) versus transformed or displaced, and design targeted learning pathways for each group.
Build change management into AI rollouts: employee buy-in and psychological safety around working alongside AI systems are as critical as technical infrastructure.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to public health education contexts and faculty development settings. Generalisability to other sectors and disciplines, or to non-academic workplace settings, is unclear without additional detail on methods and sample.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI adoption is a key barrier to building AI literacy—design development programs that address underlying concerns and anxieties rather than assuming readiness.

Structured faculty development is essential to shift educators from resistance to readiness; consider phased programs that build confidence and practical capability before expecting adoption in curricula.
Public health educators need AI literacy to teach it effectively; ensure your capability-building strategy targets the educators and leaders who will model and champion AI skills to others.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — proposes a conceptual framework for higher education contexts, but empirical validation across diverse institutions and geographies is not evident from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Consider adopting a four-domain model of AI literacy (likely spanning technical understanding, ethical reasoning, application skills, and strategic thinking) rather than treating AI literacy as a single skill — this meta-skill approach may better prepare academic leaders for innovation.
Apply this framework to design targeted AI literacy programs for management and leadership roles in your organisation, ensuring each domain is addressed systematically rather than ad hoc training.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The rise of AI in the workplace: why perceived organizational support fails to protect long-term career satisfaction - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The rise of AI in the workplace: why perceived organizational support fails to protect long-term career satisfaction  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited information available from title and snippet alone; generalisability cannot be fully assessed without access to full methodology, sample characteristics, and geographic scope.
takeaways: Perceived organizational support (POS) around AI implementation may not be sufficient to sustain career satisfaction long-term — organisations need to pair support messaging with concrete career development pathways and skill-building opportunities as AI transforms roles.

Monitor career satisfaction trajectories separately from initial perceptions of support; employees may report satisfaction with support in the short term but experience declining satisfaction if their actual career prospects or role autonomy decline due to AI integration.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - Nature
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to nursing contexts and may not generalise to other professions or sectors. The three-wave design strengthens causal inference, but geographic scope and sample size are unclear from the snippet alone.
takeaways: When introducing medical AI to nursing teams, prioritise preserving and enhancing work autonomy — staff who retain meaningful control over how they use AI tools show better wellbeing outcomes than those who experience AI as externally imposed.
Design AI implementation to be a tool that nurses direct, rather than a system that directs them; this autonomy appears to be the key mechanism linking AI readiness to positive wellbeing effects.

articles.title: How AI is reshaping human skills and thinking - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: How AI is reshaping human skills and thinking  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Moderate — represents a professional association perspective on AI's cognitive impact, but lacks empirical data or specific evidence base. Insights are applicable across English-speaking contexts but grounded in US psychological research traditions.
takeaways: AI is reshaping which cognitive skills remain valuable in the workplace — focus development efforts on uniquely human capabilities (critical thinking, emotional intelligence, complex problem-solving) rather than routine analytical tasks.

Psychological evidence shows humans adapt thinking patterns when working alongside AI systems; managers should actively monitor how team members are adjusting their approach to work and provide scaffolding to prevent over-reliance on AI outputs.

Consider psychological safety implications: employees may worry about skill obsolescence or AI replacing their roles — address these concerns explicitly rather than assuming people will naturally adapt.

articles.title: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear without access to full article — appears to examine how role ambiguity and self-efficacy affect employee engagement with generative AI, but sample size, geography, and sector composition are not evident from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Role clarity around AI responsibilities matters: employees uncertain about their role in AI collaboration may be less willing to adopt or effectively use generative AI tools — clarifying expectations and boundaries upfront can reduce this barrier.

Self-efficacy is a key lever: investing in training and confidence-building around AI use (not just technical skills, but belief in one's ability to use it effectively) is likely to drive higher adoption and better human-AI collaboration outcomes.

Target interventions at the intersection: employees experiencing both high role ambiguity AND low self-efficacy may be particularly disengaged — these individuals warrant additional support and explicit role definition.

articles.title: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — theoretical framework based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox, but specific empirical scope (sample size, geography, sectors) cannot be determined from title and snippet alone. Findings may vary across organisational contexts and employee roles.
takeaways: Generative AI can either deskill employees (automation effect) or enhance their capabilities (augmentation effect) depending on how it's implemented — organisations should design AI integration to maximise augmentation through deliberate skill-building and task design rather than pure automation.

Monitor whether AI adoption is changing employee knowledge-sharing behaviours and expertise development; the paradox suggests unintended consequences (e.g., reduced knowledge retention or collaborative learning) are possible even with well-intentioned AI rollouts.

articles.title: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full article — sample location, size, and sector not evident from title. The conceptual model (AI → job insecurity, moderated by self-efficacy and leadership) is likely applicable across sectors and geographies, but empirical support depends on sample characteristics.
takeaways: Transformational leadership and employee self-efficacy can buffer job insecurity when AI is introduced — focus leadership development and capability-building alongside AI rollout to reduce anxiety and resistance.

AI implementation should pair technical adoption with targeted interventions to strengthen employee confidence in their adaptability; organisations ignoring self-efficacy risk higher disengagement and turnover during AI transitions.

Leaders introducing AI tools should explicitly communicate how roles will evolve and invest in upskilling to activate the protective effects of both leadership style and employee belief in their ability to cope with change.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte's framework is based on consulting experience across clients but specific sample size, sectors, and geographies are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Shift from 'adoption' (one-time implementation) to 'adaptation' (ongoing behavioural change) as the mental model for AI integration — this requires sustained focus on building new habits and mindsets rather than treating AI as a project with an end date.

Design change interventions around the specific human behaviours AI deployment requires (e.g. comfort with algorithmic recommendations, willingness to challenge outputs) rather than assuming technology deployment alone will drive behaviour change.

Use a structured change approach that systematically identifies behaviour gaps, designs targeted interventions to close them, and builds accountability — treating human capability development as a core deliverable, not an afterthought.

articles.title: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — geographic scope and sample characteristics not evident. The theoretical framework (JD-R model and cognitive appraisal theory) is widely applicable, but findings' generalisability depends on study design and participant demographics not described here.
takeaways: AI awareness can trigger two distinct pathways to job crafting: one through stress appraisal (threat vs. challenge perception) and one through job demands-resources fit — understanding which pathway activates in your workforce helps target interventions more effectively.

Employees' cognitive appraisal of AI (whether they view it as threatening or challenging) is malleable; managers can influence job crafting outcomes by reframing AI as a challenge rather than a threat during change communication.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified empirical data or geographic scope. Findings may reflect US business school viewpoint and may not generalise to Australian organisational contexts or non-English-speaking regions.
takeaways: Identify specific workflow tasks in your organisation where AI can augment (rather than replace) employee capabilities, then design targeted upskilling interventions before implementation to reduce resistance and build confidence.

Use AI adoption as a trigger for behaviour change: frame it as an opportunity to retire outdated processes and habits, making the transition period a natural reset point for new ways of working rather than simply layering AI onto existing practices.

Establish clear communication about which roles will change versus which will be created or transformed, as ambiguity about job security is a primary barrier to employee engagement with AI tools — specificity drives adoption behaviour.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey analysis draws on global client work and industry trends, but findings reflect consulting practice experience rather than rigorous empirical research. Applicability may vary by sector, organisational maturity, and local context.
takeaways: Structure AI transformation into distinct phases (adoption → scaling → business impact) to set realistic timelines and milestones; this helps leaders avoid expecting immediate ROI and manage stakeholder expectations during the critical middle phase.

Use McKinsey's three-horizon framework to diagnose where your organisation sits and identify the specific behaviour and capability gaps blocking progress to the next horizon—not all organisations need the same interventions.
Focus on embedding AI literacy and decision-making practices *during* the adoption phase, not after, so teams develop the mental models needed to scale impact rather than simply deploying tools.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited generalisability — unable to assess from snippet alone. Likely limited to specific organizational contexts and industries where the study was conducted; geographic scope unclear.
takeaways: When introducing AI tools, frame adoption as creating new opportunities (approach-oriented messaging) rather than threatening existing roles, as employee responses to AI vary significantly based on psychological framing.

Monitor and design job crafting interventions during AI rollout — employees may actively reshape their roles in response to AI, and proactive support can direct this toward skill-building and engagement rather than withdrawal.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG analysis draws on consulting engagements and industry trends, but lacks transparent methodology and sample details. Findings likely skew toward large enterprises in developed economies that can afford consulting services.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability challenge, not just a technology implementation—success requires deliberate skill-building, role redesign, and change management alongside technical deployment.
Identify which job functions will change versus disappear, then design targeted upskilling pathways and communication strategies to reduce anxiety and build employee buy-in during transition periods.
Establish clear accountability for workforce readiness (e.g., manager training, job redesign timelines) as part of your AI governance, not as an afterthought once systems are live.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unknown — snippet does not provide study details, sample characteristics, or geographic scope. Read full article to assess validity and applicability.
takeaways: People high in antagonistic narcissism (dominance-seeking, argumentative traits) may have unexpected dating success, possibly because confidence and assertiveness read as attractive in initial romantic contexts.

This finding is counterintuitive because narcissism is typically associated with poor long-term relationship outcomes — suggesting a mismatch between what attracts people romantically and what sustains healthy partnerships.

The result highlights how personality traits attractive in courtship differ from those needed for relationship quality, making it a fun reminder that first impressions and lasting compatibility aren't the same thing.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title and snippet — geographic location, sample size, and participant demographics are unknown.
takeaways: People with different personality traits don't all remember surprising events equally well — your personality shapes what sticks in your memory.
This challenges the idea that shock alone guarantees memory — it's the interaction between who you are and what surprises you that determines whether you'll actually remember it.
An intriguing window into why two people can witness the same shocking moment and walk away with completely different memories of it.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — generalisability depends on sample size, participant selection criteria, and neuroimaging methodology, which are not detailed in the provided snippet.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies suggest psychopathic traits correlate with measurable neurobiological differences, challenging the idea that psychopathy is purely behavioural or environmental.

The framing of findings as 'shocking' highlights how neuroscience discoveries about personality disorders can shift public perception — what seems surprising often reflects how little we knew before, not how unusual the trait actually is.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — sample size, geographic scope, and methodology not detailed. Generalisability depends on the wine review dataset used and whether findings hold across different wine cultures and reviewing populations.
takeaways: Wine review language patterns can reveal personality traits — people's tasting notes and descriptors reflect deeper aspects of who they are, not just their palate preferences.
AI text analysis can uncover hidden personality signals in everyday writing, suggesting our word choices in reviews, emails, and casual writing leak information about our psychological profiles.

This quirky finding shows how machine learning can find unexpected patterns in cultural data (wine reviews) that humans might never spot — bridging food/wine culture with personality psychology in a surprising way.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited to twin study methodology, which requires specific participant availability and assumptions about equal environments; geographic scope unclear from snippet alone, likely restricts generalisability to jurisdictions where twin registries are well-established.
takeaways: Twin studies reveal that authoritarian political beliefs have a meaningful genetic component, surprising people who assume ideology is purely learned — this challenges the intuition that politics is purely about upbringing or experience.

The finding that nature and nurture both shape authoritarianism suggests the political worldviews people develop aren't simply inherited from parents through messaging, making the roots of political polarisation more biologically grounded than pop psychology often assumes.

articles.title: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors? - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors?  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — synthesises existing research on MBTI's predictive validity, but findings depend heavily on the quality and diversity of studies reviewed; MBTI's cross-cultural applicability remains contested.
takeaways: The MBTI is surprisingly poor at predicting actual leadership behaviours — a tool trusted by millions of organisations worldwide has limited scientific support for what it claims to do.

Despite decades of popularity in corporate settings, personality typing based on four dichotomies oversimplifies the complexity of leadership, making it an entertaining party trick rather than a reliable management tool.

The gap between MBTI's widespread adoption and its weak empirical foundation highlights how easily organizations adopt appealing ideas without rigorous evidence — a fascinating case study in organizational mythology.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — likely based on a specific sample with unclear geographic scope and sector representation; findings about the relationship between inclusive leadership, psychological safety, and innovation may vary across cultural contexts with different power distance orientations.
takeaways: Leaders who combine inclusive practices with awareness of their own power-distance orientation can more effectively build psychological safety, which in turn unlocks team innovation — assess your leadership style and actively create conditions where team members feel safe voicing ideas regardless of hierarchy.

Psychological safety acts as a mechanism linking inclusive leadership to innovation outcomes — intentionally foster it through practices like inviting dissenting views, admitting uncertainty, and responding non-defensively to challenge.

Power distance orientation (the extent to which leaders accept hierarchy) moderates these relationships — calibrate your inclusive leadership approach based on team members' cultural expectations about authority, rather than assuming one style fits all.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Moderate to high — PwC surveys typically reach large, geographically diverse samples across multiple sectors, though respondents tend to skew toward professional/white-collar workers and may not fully represent frontline or non-English-speaking workforces.
takeaways: Identify which psychological safety concerns (e.g., fear of job displacement, anxiety about AI adoption, concerns about speaking up) are most prevalent among your workforce by comparing your organisation's data against PwC's global baseline.

Use PwC's findings on workforce hopes and fears to design targeted interventions — for example, if data shows fear of automation is high, proactively communicate how AI will augment rather than replace roles, and create safe forums for employees to ask questions and express concerns.

Benchmark your organisation's psychological safety metrics and employee sentiment on AI/technology adoption against PwC's global trends to identify where your culture is stronger or weaker, and prioritise culture-building in underperforming areas.

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.sample: Academic teams (geographic scope not specified in snippet)
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings are specific to academic settings and multicultural team contexts; generalisability to corporate or other organisational environments unclear from snippet provided.
takeaways: AI-assisted tools may help leaders identify and reduce gender-based inclusion gaps in diverse teams; consider piloting structured feedback or bias-detection systems to audit team participation and psychological safety outcomes by gender.

Inclusive leadership practices that leverage AI could complement rather than replace human judgment — use AI insights to prompt reflection on whose voices are heard in meetings and decisions, then adjust facilitation practices accordingly.

Monitor whether AI-assisted inclusion efforts actually improve psychological safety for underrepresented groups (e.g. women in STEM teams), not just surface-level diversity metrics, to ensure genuine cultural change.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — study design and sample characteristics not clear from title/snippet alone; findings may not generalise across all organisational contexts, industries, or geographic regions without access to full methodology.
takeaways: AI adoption without concurrent attention to psychological safety can negatively impact employee mental health; leaders should assess and strengthen psychological safety before or alongside AI implementation.

Ethical leadership is a critical moderating factor in the AI adoption–wellbeing relationship; organisations should ensure leaders model and communicate clear ethical principles around AI use to mitigate depression and disengagement.

When rolling out AI, audit whether employees feel safe speaking up about concerns, fears, or mistakes related to the technology; psychological safety interventions (e.g. normalising questions, rewarding voice) are preventive measures against mental health decline.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Limited — BCG report likely draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample composition, methodology, and geographic scope are not evident from the title and snippet alone. Generalisability depends on whether findings are backed by original research or synthesise existing literature.
takeaways: Psychological safety can function as an equity mechanism — creating space where historically marginalised or quieter employees feel confident contributing ideas without fear of embarrassment or retribution, helping organisations tap into overlooked talent and perspectives.

Consider auditing whose voices are heard in your team meetings and decision-making forums; psychological safety interventions (e.g., soliciting input from quieter team members, normalising admitting uncertainty, leading with vulnerability) may reveal performance gaps and unlock hidden capability.

articles.title: Reframing workplace safety, wellbeing, and performance among operating room nurses in contemporary healthcare systems - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Reframing workplace safety, wellbeing, and performance among operating room nurses in contemporary healthcare systems  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on operating room nurses in healthcare settings; findings may not generalise to other high-risk or non-clinical workplaces without further validation.
takeaways: Reframing safety and wellbeing as interconnected rather than separate concerns may improve both psychological safety and clinical performance in high-stress environments like operating theatres.

Healthcare organisations should assess how current safety protocols affect nurse wellbeing and psychological safety; addressing burnout and fear of reporting errors directly supports safer clinical practice.
